In the open autoregressive regime, temporal trace summaries retain selective utility and useful ranking evidence is already present in early prefixes. In the hosted black-box regime, however, combining behavioral signals with verbalized confidence does not improve the primary AURC endpoint ($\Delta$AURC $-0.0030$, 95\% CI [$-0.0151$, $0.0102$]).

Autoregressive language models expose a natural sequence of conditional next-token distributions, and prior work studies whether confidence, entropy, self-consistency, or semantic disagreement can predict when a generated answer is wrong \citep{jiang2021know,kuhn2023semantic,farquhar2024semantic,kapoor2024taught}.

claims.claim_text: Recent decoding work also shows that confidence trajectories are operationally useful in dLLMs. One-shot dynamic thresholding adapts parallel-decoding cutoffs from observed confidence trajectories \citep{shen2025osdt}, while CD4LM uses confidence-adaptive decoding to allocate inference effort \citep{liang2026cd4lm}. STDec exploits spatial and temporal token-prediction stability to accelerate commitment \citep{chen2026stdec}, and PACE-dLLM fits per-step confidence cliffs to choose an elastic look-ahead horizon \citep{lu2026pacedllm}. These methods use trajectory structure to improve decoding efficiency; our objective is different: we test whether frozen pre-outcome dynamics add held-out information about answer-level error beyond matched decision-time entropy. DiffuGuard further reports that intra-step and inter-step denoising dynamics can matter for safety failures \citep{li2025diffuguard}.
claims.source_field: frozen protocol, artifact, and provenance bindings

claims.claim_text: DiSE estimates sequence-level confidence by asking the dLLM to regenerate tokens in its completed output and also uses self-evaluation to control generation length \citep{zhong2026dise}. Vazhentsev et al. provide a systematic dLLM-UQ study over LLaDA and Dream, including trajectory entropy and likelihood, commitment confidence, remasking and token-flip statistics, denoising complexity, and trajectory-semantic dissimilarity; they evaluate selective rejection and efficiency against broad UQ baselines \citep{vazhentsev2026dllmuq}. Yadav et al. identify a representation--confidence gap under noisy inputs, showing that visible confidence can lose ranking quality even when hidden representations retain useful error information \citep{yadav2026unsure}. These works establish that dLLM-specific confidence and trajectory signals are meaningful. \method therefore does not claim that trajectory-based dLLM uncertainty, confidence evolution, or trajectory-triggered intervention is new. Instead, it isolates complementary questions: whether a fixed telemetry vector from one native generation supplies \emph{incremental} held-out error information beyond matched decision-time entropy, whether that information improves selective decisions, and whether it allocates additional inference compute more effectively than matched random allocation at an explicitly reported cost.

claims.claim_text: Semantic uncertainty aggregates meaning-equivalent generations and can outperform lexical uncertainty for open-ended QA \citep{kuhn2023semantic,farquhar2024semantic}; kernel language entropy and semantic density refine this sampling-based view in continuous semantic spaces \citep{nikitin2024kernel,qiu2024density}. MARS reweights token-level sequence likelihood by semantic contribution \citep{bakman2024mars}, while ConU combines sampling-based uncertainty with conformal calibration for open-ended generation \citep{wang2024conu}. These methods motivate our calibrated and repeated-sampling baselines. Our primary comparison is deliberately nested and single-run: decision-time entropy and the trajectory-augmented model are calibrated identically and scored on exactly the same held-out examples.

\paragraph{Evidence.} On the complete registered 12-cell subset, \method improves AURC by \RepeatedDeltaAURC\ (95\% CI [\RepeatedDeltaAURCLow, \RepeatedDeltaAURCHigh]) and AUPRC by \RepeatedDeltaAUPRC\ (95\% CI [\RepeatedDeltaAUPRCLow, \RepeatedDeltaAUPRCHigh]). The AUROC difference is \RepeatedDeltaAUROC\ (95\% CI [\RepeatedDeltaAUROCLow, \RepeatedDeltaAUROCHigh]), which is statistically unresolved. Calibration moves in the opposite direction: ECE15 improvement is \RepeatedDeltaECE\ (95\% CI [\RepeatedDeltaECELow, \RepeatedDeltaECEHigh]) and NLL improvement is \RepeatedDeltaNLL\ (95\% CI [\RepeatedDeltaNLLLow, \RepeatedDeltaNLLHigh]); negative values favor repeated sampling under the registered improvement direction.
\caption{Five-sample comparison on the pre-specified \RepeatedCellCount-cell ($3\times\RepeatedDatasetCount$) subset. AURC is lower-is-better; the other columns are higher-is-better.}

Using fixed seed prefixes of the existing samples, we evaluate the repeated-sampling baseline at $K\in\{2,3,5\}$ without new generation. AUROC rises from \RQTwoKTwoAUROC{} to \RQTwoKThreeAUROC{} to \RQTwoKFiveAUROC{}, while AURC falls from \RQTwoKTwoAURC{} to \RQTwoKThreeAURC{} to \RQTwoKFiveAURC{} as auxiliary time rises from \RQTwoKTwoSeconds{} to \RQTwoKThreeSeconds{} to \RQTwoKFiveSeconds{} seconds per example. ECE$_{15}$ moves oppositely (\RQTwoKTwoECE{}, \RQTwoKThreeECE{}, \RQTwoKFiveECE{}). Figure~\ref{fig:rq2-cost-utility} presents this cost--utility pattern; Appendix~\ref{tab:rq2-sample-efficiency} provides the complete numerical sensitivity. This analysis is secondary and does not select a new stopping policy.

\caption{Secondary RQ2 cost--utility sensitivity over $K=2,3,5$. Increasing $K$ improves average error ranking and selective risk over the three fixed operating points, but costs more auxiliary time and worsens ECE$_{15}$.}

\paragraph{Evidence.} At the primary 50\% cap, the policy attains accuracy \AdaptiveAccuracy\ versus \AdaptiveBaseAccuracy\ at base budget: a gain of \AdaptiveDeltaBase\ (95\% CI [\AdaptiveDeltaBaseLow, \AdaptiveDeltaBaseHigh]). It also exceeds matched-random allocation by \AdaptiveDeltaRandom\ (95\% CI [\AdaptiveDeltaRandomLow, \AdaptiveDeltaRandomHigh]). The difference from full refinement is \AdaptiveDeltaRefined\ (95\% CI [\AdaptiveDeltaRefinedLow, \AdaptiveDeltaRefinedHigh]) and is unresolved. The policy selects \AdaptiveSelectedFraction\ of examples, costs \AdaptiveCost\ times base, and uses \AdaptiveCostToFull\ of full-refinement compute.

\paragraph{Boundary.} The 25\% and 75\% caps are sensitivity analyses, not competing primary endpoints. They attain accuracy \AdaptiveSensitivityTwentyFiveAccuracy\ at \AdaptiveSensitivityTwentyFiveCost$\times$ base (selected fraction \AdaptiveSensitivityTwentyFiveSelectedFraction) and \AdaptiveSensitivitySeventyFiveAccuracy\ at \AdaptiveSensitivitySeventyFiveCost$\times$ base (selected fraction \AdaptiveSensitivitySeventyFiveSelectedFraction), respectively. The experiment tests two frozen budgets and cannot justify arbitrary dynamic schedules.

\caption{Primary adaptive second-pass evaluation at the pre-specified 50\% selection cap. The full-refinement comparison is descriptive; its direct difference from \method is statistically unresolved.}

\paragraph{Design.} The pinned Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct control uses the same tasks and partitions. Within-regime comparisons use mean token entropy as the matched endpoint baseline; five-sample semantic disagreement provides a higher-cost comparator. Seeds, sampling settings, token limits, telemetry, model revision, and hypotheses were fixed before outcome scoring.

\paragraph{Evidence and answer.} All three directional gates are met after Holm correction. Within the open AR control, the trace calibrator improves AURC over mean token entropy by 0.0343 (95\% CI [0.0189, 0.0501]); its macro AUROC is 0.6889 versus 0.6433 for mean token entropy. Five-sample semantic disagreement is stronger in the reported macro comparison (AURC 0.2787; AUROC 0.7817) but requires multiple generations. Thus, temporal trace summaries remain useful without revision, while repeated sampling provides additional evidence at higher inference cost.

\paragraph{Secondary exploratory actionability.} A pre-specified prefix analysis uses only stored token telemetry and scored outcomes, with no new generation. At 25\%, 50\%, 75\%, and 100\% of each generated trace, the trajectory model improves AURC over the matched endpoint-only prefix model by 0.0660 (95\% CI [0.0569, 0.0752]), 0.0765 [0.0679, 0.0849], 0.0829 [0.0733, 0.0923], and 0.0881 [0.0802, 0.0958], respectively. These fixed-fraction results show that useful ranking information is already present in early AR prefixes; they do not define or optimize a stopping threshold and cannot modify H4a--H4c.

Native trajectory telemetry adds held-out ranking information beyond a matched decision-time endpoint, but that information does not improve every uncertainty objective. Under abstention, its AURC and AUPRC gains coexist with worse ECE$_{15}$ and NLL than repeated sampling, separating selective ordering from probability calibration. When used for action, calibrated risk improves allocation of a fixed second-pass budget over matched-random refinement, although the comparison with full refinement does not establish equivalence. The practical lesson is that ranking, calibration, and compute allocation should be evaluated as distinct capabilities.

claims.claim_text: The primary execution is a selective second-pass rerun: selected examples launch a separate refined-budget generation from scratch. Therefore the nominal mean compute is $B_0+fB_1$. We do not use the cheaper $B_0+f(B_1-B_0)$ continuation formula unless a model-specific runtime actually resumes the same trajectory. We report policy accuracy, selection fraction, normalized cost relative to $B_0$, and paired bootstrap intervals for accuracy differences versus base, fully refined, and expected random second-pass refinement. The primary 50\% cap and the frozen 25\%/75\% sensitivities are each aggregated over the complete 18-cell matrix with equal cell weight and a paired class-stratified within-cell bootstrap. The 50\% cap is the sole primary endpoint. Its direct accuracy difference from full refinement has a confidence interval spanning zero, so closeness of the point estimates is not interpreted as statistical equivalence.
